summary: Describes GSMPv3, an asymmetric protocol letting external controllers set up and maintain state in label switches such as ATM, frame relay or MPLS switches. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: A boss computer tells a switch exactly how to forward traffic. This is the language they use.

questions: how does gsmp control a switch
what is the gsmp adjacency protocol
subtitle: A master-slave protocol that lets an external controller set up connections, resources and ports on a label switch.

tldr.problem: Label switches such as ATM, frame relay or MPLS switches forward traffic by exact-match labels, but something has to tell them which connections to build and which resources to reserve.
tldr.mechanism: GSMPv3 lets one or more external controllers act as masters over a switch. The controller sends request messages and the switch answers, covering connections, reservations, ports, configuration, statistics and quality of service, plus an adjacency protocol that keeps both sides in sync.
tldr.outcome: A controller can manage unicast and multicast connection state and switch resources through one protocol. GSMP packets travel over encapsulations defined in a companion document, and IP use REQUIRES TCP/IP with the security rules there.

today: RFC 3292 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2002, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the earlier GSMP versions in RFC 1987 and RFC 2297.

sections.title: What GSMP Does
sections.content:
The General Switch Management Protocol (GSMP) is a general purpose protocol to control a label switch. A controller can establish and release connections across the switch, add and delete leaves on a multicast connection, manage ports, ask for configuration, reserve switch resources and request statistics. The switch can also tell the controller about asynchronous events such as a link going down.

The protocol is asymmetric: the controller is the master and the switch is the slave. One controller can run the protocol over separate control connections to several switches, and a switch can have more than one controller by using partitions. A physical switch is split into virtual switches before GSMP runs, and each partition has a one-to-one control relationship with its own logical controller.

A switch has ports, each with an input and an output side. Each port supports one label type, and label types include ATM, Frame Relay, MPLS Generic and FEC labels. A connection joins one incoming labelled channel to one or more outgoing ones. GSMP supports point-to-point and point-to-multipoint connections.
sections.plainLanguage: A boss computer tells a switch which roads to connect. One big switch can be cut into smaller pretend-switches, each with its own boss.

sections.title: Controller, Switch and Message Classes
sections.content:
Every exchange follows the same pattern. The controller sends a request that says whether a reply is wanted and carries a transaction identifier. The switch replies with success or failure. Unless stated otherwise, a failure response is identical to the request that failed, with the Code field saying why.

There are six classes of request-response message: Connection Management, Reservation Management, Port Management, State and Statistics, Configuration, and Quality of Service. The switch may also send asynchronous Event messages, which the controller does not acknowledge unless asked to, and there is a separate adjacency protocol message.

Switch ports are named by a 32-bit port number chosen by the switch, whose internal structure is opaque to GSMP. Each port also has a port session number. A message with the wrong one MUST be rejected, which lets the controller notice a link failure and stay synchronised. GSMP packets can travel over any suitable medium, and encapsulations for ATM, Ethernet and TCP are specified in RFC 3293.
sections.plainLanguage: The boss sends a note with a number on it, and the switch answers with the same number so the boss knows which note it answers. The switch can also shout out when something breaks.

sections.title: The Common Message Format and Labels
sections.content:
Every GSMP message except the adjacency message starts with the same header: Version, Message Type, Result, Code, Partition ID, a Transaction Identifier, an I flag with a SubMessage Number, and Length. The message body follows.

The Result field says whether a reply is needed in requests (NoSuccessAck = 1, AckAll = 2) and reports the outcome in responses (Success = 3, Failure = 4, More = 5). ReturnReceipt = 6 is used in events that need acknowledgement. More and the SubMessage Number let a message be split when it exceeds the link's MTU. Unused or reserved fields MUST be set to zero by the sender and ignored by the receiver, and a success response MUST NOT be sent until the operation has completed.

Labels use a type-length-value (TLV) layout. The types defined are the ATM Label (0x100), FR Label (0x101), MPLS Gen Label (0x102) and FEC Label (0x103).
sections.plainLanguage: Every message begins with the same envelope: what kind of message it is, a ticket number, and how long it is. After that comes the actual note.

sections.title: Connections, Reservations and Management
sections.content:
The main connection message is Add Branch (Message Type 16). It sets up a connection or adds a branch to an existing one. The connection is named by an input port and input label, the branch by an output port and output label, and quality of service by selector fields. Other connection messages are Delete Tree (18), Delete Branches (17), Delete All Input (20), Delete All Output (21), Move Output Branch (22) and Move Input Branch (23); Verify Tree (19) is listed as obsoleted.

Reservation messages (70 to 72) request and delete reservations of switch resources. The Port Management message (32) can bring a port into service, take it out, loop it back, reset it or change its transmit rate. Configuration messages (64 to 67) report the switch, its ports and the services it offers. State and Statistics messages (48 to 52) report connection activity and counters.

Quality of service uses a default configuration that every switch MUST support, with three models: a Service Model (based on external definitions such as Integrated Services or ATM Service Categories), a Simple Abstract Model with strict priorities, and a QoS Profile Model for externally defined semantics such as Differentiated Services behaviours. A switch may support alternative configurations that the controller can negotiate.
sections.plainLanguage: The boss can say connect road A to road B, close this road, give this lane to ambulances, or tell me how busy you are.

sections.title: The Adjacency Protocol
sections.content:
GSMP is a hard state protocol, so each side must notice quickly when contact is lost or the other side changes. The adjacency protocol (Message Type 10) synchronises state, agrees on the protocol version, discovers the identity of the entity at the other end and detects when it changes. No other GSMP messages may cross the link until it has achieved synchronisation, and messages received without synchronisation MUST be discarded.

Its messages have four codes: SYN = 1, SYNACK = 2, ACK = 3 and RSTACK = 4. In a SYN the Version field carries the highest version the sender understands; the receiver replies with a SYNACK carrying a version it supports. This specification is Version 3. An M-flag marks the sender as master or slave so that two masters or two slaves do not synchronise. The Timer field announces the time between periodic messages in units of 100 ms.

If no valid GSMP message arrives for more than three times the announced timer, loss of synchronisation may be declared. A switch SHOULD keep its connection state meanwhile, then reset it if PFLAG = 1 (a new adjacency) or retain it if PFLAG = 2 (adjacency re-established). Several controllers may share one partition, but they must coordinate themselves, and an Adjacency Update event tells each of them about the others.
sections.plainLanguage: Before they talk about real work, the boss and the switch shake hands and keep saying hello. If the hellos stop, they know something is wrong and start over.

sections.title: Failure Codes
sections.content:
A failure response carries one of a list of codes, such as 1 (unspecified reason), 2 (invalid request message), 3 (request not implemented on this switch), 4 (a specified port does not exist), 5 (invalid port session number), 6 (a specified port is down), 7 (invalid partition ID), 11 (the connection does not exist), 12 (the branch does not exist), 13 and 14 (invalid input or output label), and 18 and 19 (insufficient resources, out of resources). Further codes cover reservations and ATM virtual path rules.

Failure always comes with the request's own transaction identifier, so the controller can tell which request failed.
sections.plainLanguage: If the switch cannot do what it was asked, it sends the request back with a number saying why, like a teacher handing back homework with a note.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The security section is short. The security of GSMP's TCP/IP control channel is addressed in RFC 3293, and for every use of GSMP over an IP network it is REQUIRED that GSMP run over TCP/IP using the security considerations discussed there.

Appendix B sets up IANA name spaces for message types, label types, results, failure response codes, adaptation types, model types, port types, service IDs, traffic controls and event flags. Message Types 0 to 99 belong to the base protocol and are allocated by IETF consensus.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC says that when GSMP is sent over the internet it must use the safe TCP setup described in a companion document.

fields.name: Version
fields.desc: GSMP version negotiated by the adjacency protocol.

fields.name: Message Type
fields.desc: Message class and type, for example 16 for Add Branch.

fields.name: Result
fields.desc: Whether an ack is wanted, or the outcome of a response.

fields.name: Code
fields.desc: Further detail, mostly an error code in failures.

fields.name: Partition ID
fields.desc: Associates the message with a switch partition.

fields.name: Transaction Identifier
fields.desc: Matches a response to its request.

fields.name: I
fields.desc: Says what the SubMessage Number means.

fields.name: SubMessage Number
fields.desc: Position of a segment, or total segment count.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the message including its header.

items.label: Add Branch
items.desc: Set up a connection or add a branch.

items.label: Port Management
items.desc: Bring a port up, take it down, loop back or reset.
